## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-06.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
CPU Socket

The CPU socket provides the connection between the processor and the motherboard.

Main socket types
LGA = Land Grid Array
PGA = Pin Grid Array
BGA = Ball Grid Array
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-07.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
LGA Socket

Characteristics
The pins are located in the socket
They connect to the contacts on the underside of the CPU

Reduces processor manufacturing cost
Stable electrical connection
Examples: LGA 775 (2004), LGA 1156 (2009),
LGA 1155 (2011), LGA 1150 (2013), LGA
1151 (2015), LGA 1200 (2020), LGA 1700
(2021), LGA 1851 (late 2025?)

Primarily used by Intel processors
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-08.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
PGA Socket

Characteristics
The pins are located on the processor
They connect to the holes in the socket

Requires more space
Less durable
Easier CPU installation
Examples: Socket A (2000), Socket AM2 (2006), Socket AM3 (2009), Socket AM1
(2014), Socket AM4 (2016)

Today, AMD also uses LGA sockets, e.g. Socket AM5 (2022)

Primarily used by AMD processors
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-09.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
BGA Socket

Characteristics
Small solder balls instead of pins
The processor is fixed in place (soldered connection)
Compact size
Not replaceable
Other components can also be integrated alongside the CPU

Examples: BGA 437 (2009), BGA 956 (2013),
BGA 1526 (2018), BGA 1787 (2021), BGA 2114 (2022), BGA (2540) ?

Primarily used in laptops and mobile devices
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-20.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
ARM Processor Architecture

64-bit RISC architecture
Manufacturers: Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Ampere, AWS
Heterogeneous cores: P-cores (performance) + E-cores (efficiency); dynamic scheduling, DVFS.
SoC integration: CPU + GPU + NPU + DSP + ISP + modem on a single chip
Ecosystem: Android, iOS, Linux, macOS, Windows on ARM.
Excellent performance per watt: dominant in mobile/IoT
increasingly competitive in laptops and servers (e.g. Apple M, AWS Graviton, Ampere).
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-21.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
What Is a CPU Core?

In multicore CPUs, each core has its own ALU, Control Unit (CU), and registers.
The cores share main memory and the system bus.
The cores share some of their resources.
This allows the CPU to execute multiple instructions simultaneously.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-22.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
What Is a CPU Thread?

In multithreaded processors, each physical core contains multiple logical processors.
Threads share the resources of the core.
The operating system treats them as physical processors.
:::

::: {.notes}
RAM

The computer's main memory

Two main types:
Static RAM (SRAM)
Does not require refreshing
Fast but expensive
Used as cache memory

•

Dynamic RAM (DRAM)

Requires refreshing
Slower than SRAM
Smaller and cheaper than SRAM
Used as main memory
:::

::: {.notes}
RAM – SIMM or DIMM

SIMM modules have a single row of contacts; DIMM modules have two.

SIMM modules
1980 – 1998
May contain SRAM and DRAM chips
Typical of 80486 and early Pentium systems

DIMM modules (2000–)
Used in modern computers
Primarily DRAM
Higher capacity and performance
DDR1–DDR5, with DDR6 coming soon
:::

::: {.notes}
Expansion Cards – ISA Bus

Characteristics:

8 MHz clock speed

::: {.notes}
Expansion Cards – VESA Bus

VESA = Video Electronis Standard Association

Characteristics:
Introduced in the early 1990s

::: {.notes}
Expansion Cards – PCI Bus

PCI = Periferial Component Interconnect

Characteristics:

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-32.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

Expansion Cards – PCI Express Bus

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-40.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Power Supply Connectors

Provide power to the motherboard, processor, fans, and some peripherals.

Power connector types:
AT (older computers, ribbon-style connector)
ATX (Advanced Technology Extended), 20/24-pin – motherboard power
EPS (Extended Power Supply), 4+4 or 8+8-pin – CPU power
PCIe – power for graphics cards and high-power expansion cards
SATA 15-pin – primarily powers storage devices
Molex (older computers, 4-pin)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-41.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Motherboard Cooling

Main motherboard components requiring cooling:
CPU → dedicated cooler (fan + heatsink, or liquid cooling).
VRM (Voltage Regulator Module) → heatsinks around the CPU to maintain stable power delivery.
Chipset → often actively cooled in older systems; usually a passive heatsink today.
M.2 SSDs → often use dedicated heatsinks because they can run hot at high speeds.

Cooling solutions:
Passive cooling → aluminium heatsinks (chipset, VRM).
Active cooling → small fan (older chipsets, high-end motherboards).
Additional cooling → liquid-cooling blocks on premium motherboards.

CPU fan

heatsink
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-42.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Fan Connectors

Older types
Molex (4-pin peripheral connector)
Powered directly from the PSU (typically 12 V).
No speed control.
Now obsolete; used with older case fans.

Modern motherboard connectors
3-pin fan connector (DC)
1: ground, 2: +12 V, 3: tachometer (speed feedback).
Controlled by voltage regulation.
4-pin fan connector (PWM)
1: ground, 2: +12 V, 3: tachometer, 4: PWM control signal.
More precise speed control and quieter operation.
Current standard for CPU and case fans.
:::

Optical Storage – CD, DVD, Blu-ray

Optical storage media in which information is encoded in the physical structure of the disc.

Image source

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-46.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Optical Storage – Advantages and Disadvantages

Advantages
Archiving and storing movies
Capacity up to 100 GB (Blu-ray XL)
Redundant data storage
Potentially long lifespan
Disadvantages
Slow (CD: 150 KB/s – Blu-ray: 216 MB/s)
Obsolete – many computers no longer include optical drives
Prone to physical damage
Future
Declining use
However: new technologies, e.g. holographic data storage
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-47.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Secondary Storage – Hard Disk Drives (HDDs)

Magnetic storage devices in which information is stored in a magnetic layer.

Image source

Typical interfaces: IDE, SATA, SCSI
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-48.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
HDD – Advantages and Disadvantages

Advantages
High capacity (up to 24 TB)
Low-cost storage
Reliable for long-term storage
Multiple interfaces: IDE, SCSI, SATA, SAS
Disadvantages
Slow (150–300 MB/s)
Sensitive to physical shock
Moving parts
Future
Servers and data centres (low cost, high capacity)
New technologies, e.g. laser-assisted writing and reading
Capacity expected to reach 30–40 TB
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-49.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Secondary Storage – SSDs

An SSD (Solid State Drive) is an internal storage device based on NAND flash memory.

NAND flash memory
Memory cells are arranged in a grid

A memory cell can store one or more bits
(SLC – Single-Level Cell, MLC, TLC, QLC)
Cells contain one or more floating-gate transistors

The state of the memory cell is determined by the presence or absence of charge on the floating gate.

Typical interfaces: SATA, M.2, U.2, PCIe
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-50.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
SSD – Advantages and Disadvantages

Advantages
Significantly faster data transfer than HDDs
No moving parts
Lower power consumption
Compact size, multiple form factors
Multiple interfaces/protocols: SATA, PCIe, NVMe, etc.
Disadvantages
Higher cost
Limited write endurance
Future
Higher speeds (PCIe) and capacities (up to 100 TB), with broader adoption
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-51.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Data Storage – What to Expect

Emergence of new memory technologies
Memristor – fast, durable, non-volatile memory bridging RAM and secondary storage
Phase-change memory (PCM) – stores 0 and 1 using phase changes in a material
STT-MRAM (Spin-Transfer Torque Magnetic RAM) – magnetic, energy-efficient, durable memory
ReRAM (Resistive RAM) – data storage based on changes in electrical resistance

Increasing data density
HAMR (Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording) and MAMR (Microwave-Assisted Magnetic Recording) for HDDs
Holographic storage – 3D laser-based storage with theoretical TB–PB capacities

New theoretical directions
Quantum data storage – using quantum bits (qubits)
DNA data storage – storing data in biological molecules at extremely high density and with long lifespan

Usage trends
Growth of cloud storage – supplementing or replacing local physical storage
Edge storage – handling data closer to its source (IoT, smart devices)
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-54.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Monitor Connectors

VGA (Video Graphics Array, D-Sub, analogue)
Introduced in 1987; the PC monitor standard for decades.
Analogue signal only; practical high-quality limit around Full HD.
Now obsolete, but still occasionally found on projectors.

DVI (Digital Visual Interface, digital/analogue)
Introduced in 1999 as the digital successor to VGA.
Variants: DVI-D (digital), DVI-A (analogue), DVI-I (combined).
Max. 1920×1200 (Single Link) or 2560×1600 (Dual Link).
Also being phased out.

HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface)
Introduced in 2003, primarily for TVs and home entertainment devices.
Digital video + audio over a single cable.
Still widely used today, including on monitors and laptops.
Versions include HDMI 1.4 (Full HD/4K), HDMI 2.0 (4K 60 Hz), HDMI 2.1 (8K, 120 Hz).

DisplayPort (see later) + others (Mini DisplayPort, USB-C, Thunderbolt)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-55.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface)

Primarily used to transmit audio and video between computers and monitors.

Characteristics:
Introduced: 2003
Signal: digital video + audio over one cable + additional data
Main uses: TVs, monitors, game consoles, home cinema

Main versions
HDMI 1.4 (2009) → 4K @ 30 Hz
HDMI 2.0 (2013) → 4K @ 60 Hz
HDMI 2.1 (2017) → 8K @ 60 Hz or 4K @ 120 Hz (gaming, VRR, eARC)
HDMI 2.2 (2025) → 16K @ 60 Hz, 12K @ 120 Hz, 4K @ 240 Hz; new Ultra96 cable required

Advantages
Widely adopted and compatible
Standard connector for TVs and consoles

Disadvantages
Less flexible than DisplayPort for monitors (fewer displays over one cable)
Shorter supported cable lengths at high resolutions
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-56.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
DisplayPort

Primarily used to transmit audio and video between computers and monitors.

Characteristics
Supports video signals up to 16K resolution
Daisy-chaining displays
Sharp, high-contrast image
High bandwidth (up to 77 Gb/s)
Multiple connector formats (standard, Mini DisplayPort, USB-C)

Multiple versions (1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 2.0)
Backward compatible with HDMI, DVI, and VGA via adapters

Which Is Better: DisplayPort or HDMI? – iVANKY
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-59.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
I/O Connectors

Allow external peripherals to be connected to the computer.

Older / disappearing: PS/2, VGA, serial/parallel ports
Current basics: USB-A (2.0 / 3.x), LAN (RJ-45), audio jack
Modern: USB-C, HDMI/DisplayPort, optical audio, Wi-Fi antenna
Premium: multiple LAN ports, 2.5G/10G Ethernet, Thunderbolt 3/4 (USB-C connector)

Motherboards Explained: I/O Panel
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-02/slide-60.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Jumpers

Jumpers are small plastic caps containing a U-shaped conductor. They connect or disconnect two pins, allowing switching between two fixed hardware settings.

Modern motherboards have few jumpers; typical uses include:
CPU configuration (e.g. clock speed, voltage)
Chipset configuration (e.g. bus speed)
Boot configuration (e.g. boot order)
CMOS reset
PnP
:::
